scenes.visual: Title card 'A Race Inside the Body' on a warm cream background. Flat cartoon style, no molecular structures. Colour map used for the whole film (and the second film): MICROBES = small TEAL dots; the body's DEFENSE (antibody) = a GOLD bar that rises from the bottom; MEMORY CELLS = GOLD-outlined cartoon cells with a small star; the Vienna clinics = two grey building outlines labelled 'First Clinic' and 'Second Clinic'. A DAY COUNTER box sits top right reading 'day 0' and stays visible in every race scene. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: In eighteen forty-six, mothers in one Vienna clinic died about four times as often as in the clinic next door. What could the doctors have been carrying? In the deadly clinic, doctors and students often handled bodies in autopsies. Then they examined mothers.
scenes.caption: In 1846, mothers in one Vienna clinic died about four times as often as in the clinic next door. What could the doctors have been carrying? In the deadly clinic, doctors and students often handled bodies in autopsies. Then they examined mothers.
scenes.visual: Two grey clinic buildings side by side, labelled 'First Clinic (doctors and students)' and 'Second Clinic (midwives)', with '1846' above them. Under each, a column of small mother icons; in the First Clinic column noticeably more icons fade to grey than in the Second (a label reads 'about 4 times as often'; no other numbers). A big question mark appears over a pair of cartoon hands walking from a door marked 'autopsy room' toward the First Clinic.
scenes.narration: In 1846, mothers in one Vienna clinic died about four times as often as in the clinic next door. What could the doctors have been carrying? In the deadly clinic, doctors and students often handled bodies in autopsies. Then they examined mothers.

scenes.tts: Ignaz Semmelweis suspected the examiners' hands. In eighteen forty-seven he had them wash in chlorine. You will test his records yourself in the lesson. But notice what he did not know. He could not name what was on those hands.
scenes.caption: Ignaz Semmelweis suspected the examiners' hands. In 1847 he had them wash in chlorine. You will test his records yourself in the lesson. But notice what he did not know. He could not name what was on those hands.
scenes.visual: Name tag 'Ignaz Semmelweis' appears. The cartoon hands dip into a basin labelled 'chlorine, 1847'. A clipboard labelled 'his records: you check them in the lesson' slides past face down, so no numbers show. Over the hands a thought bubble reads '???' with a small 'cause unknown' tag.
scenes.narration: Ignaz Semmelweis suspected the examiners' hands. In 1847 he had them wash in chlorine. You will test his records yourself in the lesson. But notice what he did not know. He could not name what was on those hands.

scenes.tts: Germ theory later gave the answer. Many diseases are caused by microbes, living things too small to see without a microscope. A microbe or virus that causes disease is called a pathogen. Many pathogens multiply once they get into the body.
scenes.visual: The '???' bubble zooms in under a cartoon microscope lens and resolves into a few TEAL dots, labelled 'microbes'. One TEAL dot gets a red-outlined tag 'pathogen: causes disease'. It slips through a gap in a skin-coloured band labelled 'into the body'.
scenes.narration: Germ theory later gave the answer. Many diseases are caused by microbes, living things too small to see without a microscope. A microbe or virus that causes disease is called a pathogen. Many pathogens multiply once they get into the body.

scenes.tts: One becomes two, two become four, and the doubling keeps going. Meanwhile the body builds a defense. Antibodies are proteins that stick to one small part of an antigen. That can block a microbe or its toxin. The first time the body meets a pathogen, building them often takes a week or more.
scenes.visual: Race view, held for the rest of the film: a TEAL curve of microbe numbers climbs steeply on the left axis, drawn from a computed doubling (each step doubles), the y axis unlabelled except 'microbes (relative, schematic scale)'. The DAY COUNTER ticks 'day 1, day 2, ...'. On the right a GOLD bar labelled 'defense (antibody)' rises slowly. Small gold Y-shaped cartoons labelled 'antibodies' cling to one bump on each TEAL dot.
scenes.narration: One becomes two, two become four, and the doubling keeps going. Meanwhile the body builds a defense. Antibodies are proteins that stick to one small part of an antigen. That can block a microbe or its toxin. The first time the body meets a pathogen, building them often takes a week or more.

scenes.tts: So picture an infection as a race. Microbes multiply, and defenses catch up. In this simple model, the microbes fall once the gold bar arrives. But by then they have climbed very high. In many infections, more microbes means a sicker person.
scenes.visual: The DAY COUNTER reaches 'day 7' as the GOLD bar reaches full height; the TEAL curve peaks and turns down. A bracket marks the tall peak, labelled 'peak'. A small sick-face icon sits beside the peak with a tag 'often more illness'. Caption strip: 'infection as a race (simple model)'.
scenes.narration: So picture an infection as a race. Microbes multiply, and defenses catch up. In this simple model, the microbes fall once the gold bar arrives. But by then they have climbed very high. In many infections, more microbes means a sicker person.

scenes.tts: There are two ways to get ahead. The first is to start the race with fewer microbes. Hand washing, clean water and sterile tools keep microbes out or leave fewer. Run the race again with a smaller start. The defense still arrives on the same day, but the peak is lower.
scenes.visual: Rewind. Icons for 'hand washing', 'clean water' and 'sterile tools' sweep away most TEAL dots at the starting line, leaving a few. The race replays: the new TEAL curve has the same shape but sits lower, under a faint ghost of the first curve. The GOLD bar again arrives at 'day 7'. Label: 'smaller start (schematic)'. No numbers on the axis.
scenes.narration: There are two ways to get ahead. The first is to start the race with fewer microbes. Hand washing, clean water and sterile tools keep microbes out or leave fewer. Run the race again with a smaller start. The defense still arrives on the same day, but the peak is lower.

scenes.tts: The second way is to send the defense in early. A vaccine shows the immune system an antigen, or instructions to make one. The immune system learns to recognize a pathogen or its toxin without the full disease. During that first meeting, some immune cells become memory cells. They stay in the body long after.
scenes.visual: A syringe labelled 'vaccine' delivers harmless pieces with a TEAL bump labelled 'antigen (the part the immune system recognizes)'. Immune cells meet them; a few turn into GOLD-outlined cells with a star, labelled 'memory cells', and stay on screen at the side, ticking past a calendar.
scenes.narration: The second way is to send the defense in early. A vaccine shows the immune system an antigen, or instructions to make one. The immune system learns to recognize a pathogen or its toxin without the full disease. During that first meeting, some immune cells become memory cells. They stay in the body long after.

scenes.tts: Now the real pathogen arrives, carrying the same antigen. This is the body's second meeting. Will the gold defense arrive sooner or later than it did the first time?
scenes.visual: A TEAL pathogen with the same antigen bump enters. The race view resets to 'day 0'. The GOLD bar waits at a small starting height. A big prompt reads 'sooner or later?' with two arrows on the day axis.
scenes.narration: Now the real pathogen arrives, carrying the same antigen. This is the body's second meeting. Will the gold defense arrive sooner or later than it did the first time?

scenes.visual: Hold the race view with the prompt 'sooner or later?' and a small countdown ring. Nothing moves.

scenes.tts: Sooner. Memory cells recognize the antigen quickly, and they lead to large amounts of antibody. The defense arrives days earlier. The microbes have had less time to double, so they never climb very high.
scenes.visual: The GOLD memory B cells light up and divide; some become cells labelled 'antibody-making cells'. Many gold Y-shaped antibodies then pour out from those antibody-making cells, not from the memory cells. The GOLD bar shoots up and arrives at 'day 3' on the DAY COUNTER. The TEAL curve turns over early: a small hump beside the ghost of the tall first-meeting peak. Label: 'second meeting (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: Sooner. Memory cells recognize the antigen quickly, and they lead to large amounts of antibody. The defense arrives days earlier. The microbes have had less time to double, so they never climb very high.

scenes.tts: Hygiene shrinks the start. A vaccine moves the defense earlier. They are two ways to win the same race. A smaller start or an earlier defense keeps the peak low.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the low curve from the smaller start, tagged 'hygiene: smaller start'; right, the small early hump, tagged 'vaccine: earlier defense'. Both share one finish line. The line 'A smaller start or an earlier defense keeps the peak low.' types out across the bottom.
scenes.narration: Hygiene shrinks the start. A vaccine moves the defense earlier. They are two ways to win the same race. A smaller start or an earlier defense keeps the peak low.

scenes.visual: End card: the Hex mascot holding a tiny stopwatch beside the line 'A smaller start or an earlier defense keeps the peak low.' A thin GOLD bar runs under the text.
